docs.title: SASjs CLI
docs.text:
The SASjs Command Line Interface is a swiss-army knife for Dev Ops on SAS Viya, SAS 9 EBI and SASjs Server.

What it does:

  • Create - scaffold a project from a template, or add the SASjs tooling to code that already exists
  • Compile - inline every dependency of each job, service and test, with the configured macro variables, init and term programs
  • Build - collate the compiled artefacts into a single deployable build pack (.json, .json.zip and .sas)
  • Deploy - create the folders, jobs, services and tests on the SAS server
  • Test - run SAS unit tests, and collect results, logs and coverage
  • Document - generate a Doxygen site from the headers in your macros and programs
  • Lint - find and fix problems in SAS code with @sasjs/lint

There is also streaming support, which lets you deploy a frontend as SAS services and skip the SAS Web Server.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
npm i -g @sasjs/cli

Node is required first - see installation.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text: If you want to run Start a new project from a template sasjs create Add SASjs to a folder that already holds SAS code sasjs init Connect the project to a SAS server sasjs add Compile, build and deploy in one step sasjs cbd

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Every command also has a page in this site; the same list is printed by sasjs help.

Command Alias What it does sasjs add Prompts for the connection details of a SAS target and saves them; sasjs add cred adds credentials to an existing target sasjs auth Obtains an access token for a target - client/secret (sasjs auth), or SAS username and password (sasjs auth login) sasjs build b Collates the compiled jobs, services and tests into a deployable build pack sasjs cb Runs compile and then build sasjs cbd Runs compile, build and then deploy sasjs compile c Inlines all dependencies into a self-contained program per job, service and test sasjs context Lists, exports, creates, edits and deletes SAS Viya compute contexts sasjs create Scaffolds a SASjs project from a template sasjs db Concatenates the .ddl and .sas files under sasjs/db into one file per database sasjs deploy d Deploys the built artefact to the target's SAS environment sasjs doc docs Generates the Doxygen documentation site, or the data lineage sasjs flow Executes a flow (a JSON list of jobs) in order, logging the results to CSV sasjs folder Creates, deletes, lists and moves SAS Viya folders sasjs fs Synchronises files with a remote SAS directory (compile, sync, deploy) sasjs help h Prints the available commands sasjs init Adds SASjs to an existing project - config, doxygen templates, lint config and @sasjs/core sasjs job Executes a SAS job on the target, with options for waiting, logging and streaming sasjs lint Lints your SAS code and reports problems, or fixes them sasjs request rq Calls a SASjs web service from the commandline sasjs run r Runs an arbitrary SAS file (local path or URL) on the target sasjs servicepack Deploys a service pack - a JSON collection of folders and services sasjs snippets Generates a VS Code snippets file from the macro Doxygen headers sasjs test Runs SAS unit tests and collects results, logs and coverage sasjs version v Prints the installed version of the CLI sasjs web w Builds the streaming web app services from the target's webSourcePath

docs.title: sasjs add
docs.text: The sasjs add command provides a series of prompts used to define a SAS target along with the relevant connection details (if SAS Viya).

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
sasjs add [options]

sasjs add cred -t targetname [options]   # add creds for an existing target
Option Alias Used by Description --target -t sasjs add cred The existing target to add credentials for. --insecure -i both Accept a TLS certificate that cannot be verified - see Insecure connections.

docs.title: Insecure connections
docs.text:
The CLI validates the TLS certificate of the server it connects to. On an estate with a self-signed certificate, or a chain that is missing its intermediate certificate, the connection fails with:

unable to verify the first certificate

Adding --insecure (alias -i) makes the requests of this command accept the certificate anyway:

sasjs add --insecure

sasjs add cred -t myTarget --insecure

The flag applies to the requests the command makes - the token request, and the server-mode check on a SASjs Server target - and it is not written to sasjsconfig.json. Later commands still validate the certificate: to make the setting permanent, put it in the target's httpsAgentOptions, and preferably fix the certificate chain as described in TLS Config.

Note

--insecure is applied from CLI 6.4.6. Earlier releases accept the flag and ignore it.

docs.title: Local or Global Config
docs.text:
The first prompt requests scope. If Local is chosen, the target configuration will be added in the /sasjs/sasjsconfig.json file, and any credentials (eg tokens) will be saved in a .env.[targetName] file in the current SASjs project directory.

If Global is chosen, the target configuration will be added to a .sasjsrc file in the users home directory. The sasjs command will look for a target here if executed outside of a SASjs project.

docs.title: Server Type
docs.text:
The second prompt requests a server type. Options:

  1. SAS Viya - works on 3.5 and 4
  2. SAS 9 - to execute code on SAS 9
  3. SASjs - for deploying to SASjs Server

docs.title: Target Name
docs.text: Choose a name for your target. Nearly every SASjs command will take this as input, so you might want to keep it short.

docs.title: Target Server URL
docs.text: This is the protocol / servername / port of your target, for instance: https://sas.sasjs.com:8080

docs.title: SAS Viya Specific
docs.text:
If SAS Viya was chosen as the server type you will be prompted for a Viya Client ID and secret - this is used for connecting to the SAS Viya REST APIs. To autogenerate these you can also check out the Viya Token Generator.

Tip

No client/secret? If you just need to run code as yourself on a dev/demo estate, you can skip this entirely and use sasjs auth login instead - it authenticates with your regular SAS username and password.

Once you have entered the client and secret, you will be given a link - click this to generate the authorisation code (one time step).

The token will eventually expire - the majority of commands will show the link again at this point to refresh the token. To avoid this happening in batch, be sure your token remains valid, eg by setting a longer expiry period.

docs.title: SAS 9 Specific
docs.text: If SAS 9 was chosen as the serverType then the server name should be chosen (eg SASApp) and the metadata repository in which to deploy the SAS Web Services. Default is Foundation.

docs.title: SASjs Artefacts
docs.text: SASjs projects are full of files with .sas extensions. With the exception of tests, the only way to tell them apart is to start from the sasjs/sasjsconfig.json file. Each file type is described below.

docs.title: Primary Artefacts
docs.text: The three Primary Artefacts are Job, Service, and Test. These artefacts are compiled, added to a build pack, and deployed to SAS.

docs.title: Job
docs.text:
A SASjs Job is a .sas program found in a directory listed in the jobFolders array of the jobConfig object. Root-level and target-level jobFolders are combined - root folders first, then target folders, duplicates removed - so a target adds job folders rather than replacing them.

Jobs are not expected to write to _webout and so are not compiled with the %webout() macro and its dependencies. Jobs are always created in a /jobs/ folder under the target appLoc.

A Job may contain:

  • Data Inputs / Outputs - used to generate the data lineage
  • Macros - listed under <h4> SAS Macros </h4>
  • SAS Includes - listed under <h4> SAS Includes </h4>
  • Binary Files - under <h4> Binary Files </h4>

docs.title: Service
docs.text:
A SASjs Service is a .sas program found in a directory listed in the serviceFolders array of the serviceConfig object. As with jobs, root-level and target-level serviceFolders are combined, root folders first, duplicates removed.

Services are expected to write to _webout and so are compiled along with the %webout() macro and dependencies. Services are always created in a /services/ folder under the target appLoc.

A Service may contain:

  • Service Inputs / Outputs - helpful for the JS developers
  • Macros - listed under <h4> SAS Macros </h4>
  • SAS Includes - listed under <h4> SAS Includes </h4>
  • Binary Files - under <h4> Binary Files </h4>

docs.title: Test
docs.text:
A SASjs Test is a .test.sas (or .test.[integer].sas) program found in ANY of the macroFolders, serviceFolders or jobFolders arrays.

Tests are compiled like services (with %webout() and dependencies) so that test results can be returned in the output JSON. Tests are always created in a /tests/ folder under the target appLoc as follows:

  • $appLoc/tests/macros -> Macro tests
  • $appLoc/tests/jobs -> Job tests
  • $appLoc/tests/services -> Service tests

A test may contain:

  • Macros - listed under <h4> SAS Macros </h4>
  • SAS Includes - listed under <h4> SAS Includes </h4>
  • Binary Files - under <h4> Binary Files </h4>

docs.title: SAS Macros
docs.text:
Macro dependencies can be specified in the following artefacts:

  • Jobs
  • Services
  • Tests
  • Macros (extracted recursively)
  • initProgram
  • termProgram

They are NOT compiled from SAS Includes or Binary Files.

To add a set of macros to a compiled file, just add the following in the header of the source file (artefact):

  <h4> SAS Macros </h4>
  @li macro1.sas
  @li macro2.sas

During compilation, these macros are sought in the following order, and the first match wins:

  • the root-level macroFolders, then the target-level ones
  • SASjs Core - the copy in the project's node_modules if the project has one, otherwise the one the CLI carries

As soon as a macro is found, the search stops. So if an mf_nobs.sas macro was placed in a directory from the root-level macroFolders array, then the same-named definition would NOT be taken from SASjs Core.

The core macros every compiled file needs (%webout(), %mf_abort() and friends) are resolved separately, from @sasjs/core. Setting the macroCorePath environment variable makes the CLI take them from that folder instead - which is how to build against a local @sasjs/core checkout. See the ENV file.

If a macro is not found then the compilation will immediately fail.

To avoid continually re-scanning the locations above, macros are added to an internal object (compileTree) as they are found, along with their dependents and source folder location. After compilation this object is exported to sasjsbuild/compileTree.json.

The compiled file does not contain duplicate macros. When compiling each Job / Service / Test, a distinct list of 'top level' macro names are taken from any initProgram and termProgram definitions, in addition to the %webout() dependencies if a Service or Test.

The header of each macro is removed in order to reduce the overall compiled file size.

docs.title: SAS Includes
docs.text:
Whilst macro definitions can be easily copy pasted into the beginning of a job, arbitrary SAS code files cannot (as they are executed immediately rather than compiled into a macro catalog).

To enable arbitrary SAS code files (SAS Includes), the compile process will wrap the code in data step put '(source code);'; statements and assign a user-provided fileref to enable the code to be easily %inc'd at the preferred point of execution.

SAS Include dependencies can be specified in the following artefacts:

  • Jobs
  • Services
  • Tests

They are NOT compiled from macros or other SAS Includes.

To add a set of SAS Includes to a compiled file, add the following in the source file (artefact) header:

  <h4> SAS Includes </h4>
  @li somefile.sas MYREF
  @li anotherfile.ddl MOJFREF

During compilation, the locations below will be searched for files named somefile.sas and anotherfile.ddl:

  • target-level programFolders array in the sasjsconfig.json file
  • root-level programFolders array in the sasjsconfig.json file

When the file is found, it is wrapped in put statements and added to the compiled file, along with a filename statement corresponding to the user-provided fileref (eg MYREF or MOJREF).

To run this code as part of your Job, Service, or Test - just execute as follows:

%inc MYREF;
%inc MOJREF;

docs.title: Binary Files
docs.text:
In rare cases you may wish to embed non textual content into your Job / Service / Test - such as Excel, Zip, Images, even video. This is all possible thanks to a common technique known as Base64 encoding. This allows ANY binary content to be represented as a text string - with the caveat that the encoded file will be at least 33% larger (4 bytes used for every 3 bytes of input).

The compilation process both base64 encodes the source file AND wraps it in put statements with a corresponding fileref for developer use.

Binary Files can be specified in the following artefacts:

  • Job
  • Service
  • Test

They are not compiled from Macros or SAS Includes.

To add a set of Binary Files to a compiled file, add the following in the source file (artefact) header:

  <h4> Binary Files </h4>
  @li myfile.zip MYZIP
  @li base.xlsx XL

During compilation, the locations below will be searched for files named myfile.zip and base.xlsx:

  • target-level binaryFolders array in the sasjsconfig.json file
  • root-level programFolders array in the sasjsconfig.json file

When the file is found, it is base64 encoded then wrapped in put statements and added to the compiled file, along with a filename statement corresponding to the user-provided fileref (eg MYZIP or XL).

To run this code as part of your Job, Service, or Test - just execute, for example, as follows:

%mp_unzip(ziploc="%sysfunc(pathname(MYZIP))",outdir=&sasjswork)

docs.title: initProgram
docs.text:
The initProgram attribute is found in the following objects:

  • jobConfig
  • serviceConfig
  • testConfig

Any Macros in the initProgram are compiled along with those in the termProgram, the Job / Service / Test itself, and the webout() macros (if a Service or Test).

The initProgram code itself is inserted without modification into the compiled file right before the main Job / Service / Test code.

Only one initProgram may be used (target level or root level), and it is always applied to ALL instances of the particular type (ie Job / Service / Test).

docs.title: termProgram
docs.text:
The termProgram attribute is found in the following objects:

  • jobConfig
  • serviceConfig
  • testConfig

Any Macros in the termProgram are compiled along with those in the initProgram, the Job / Service / Test itself, and the webout() macros (if a Service or Test).

The termProgram code itself is inserted without modification into the compiled file right after the main Job / Service / Test code.

Only one termProgram may be used (target level or root level), and it is always applied to ALL instances of the particular type (ie Job / Service / Test).

docs.title: sasjs auth
docs.text:
The sasjs auth command authenticates against a predefined SAS target. The following commands make use of authentication:

  • sasjs run
  • sasjs job execute
  • sasjs flow
  • sasjs fs
  • sasjs request
  • sasjs deploy
  • sasjs test
  • sasjs folder

The sasjs auth command has two modes:

  • sasjs auth (no subcommand) - an alias for sasjs add cred (client/secret + authorisation code flow). It is integrated also into the sasjs add command (for adding a new target).
  • sasjs auth login - authenticate with a regular SAS username and password, without needing a registered client/secret (Viya only). See below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before using this command, you will need to:

  • install the SASjs CLI
  • add a deployment target.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
sasjs auth [additional arguments]

Additional arguments may include:

  • --target (alias -t) - the target environment in which to deploy the services. If not specified, the defaultTarget will be used, as defined in sasjsconfig.json. The target can exist either in the local project configuration or in the global .sasjsrc file.
  • --insecure (alias -i) - accept a TLS certificate that cannot be verified while obtaining the token, for estates with self-signed certificates or an incomplete chain. It is not saved: later commands still validate the certificate unless the target sets httpsAgentOptions - see TLS Config. Applied from CLI 6.4.6; earlier releases accept the flag and ignore it.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Targets can have local (to a project) or global (to a user) scope. For a local target, credentials are stored in a .env.[target name] file. To have one file that covers all (local) targets you can rename this file to .env.

All published SASjs projects (and templates) already include this file in the .gitignore file, if you are deploying to your own existing project you should do the same - to prevent accidentally pushing credentials to source control.

For global targets the credentials are stored in the .sasjsrc file in the users home directory.

docs.title: Server Type
docs.text: The authentication approach taken will depend on the serverType (SASVIYA, SAS9 or SASJS).

docs.title: SAS Viya Authentication
docs.text:
There are two ways to authenticate with SAS Viya:

  1. sasjs auth login (recommended for developers) - sign in with your regular SAS username and password. No client/secret is needed. See sasjs auth login below.
  2. sasjs auth (client/secret) - an administrator provides a CLIENT and SECRET with the authorization_code grant type. Further information on this topic is available here. This remains the recommended approach for CI pipelines.

After you provide the client / secret, you are given a link which you must click to obtain the authorisation code. Be sure to select any scopes (such as openid) if presented.

Once you provide the authorisation code, the ACESS_TOKEN and REFRESH_TOKEN are saved and used for further connection requests. If the ACCESS_TOKEN expires (by default after 12 hours) the REFRESH_TOKEN will be used automatically to update, until it also expires (by default after 30 days). At this point, you will need to run sasjs auth once again.

docs.title: sasjs auth login
docs.text:
Warning

This flow uses the OAuth2 resource owner password credentials grant, which is deprecated in OAuth 2.1. It is intended for dev/demo estates where obtaining a registered client/secret is impractical. For CI pipelines and production use, use a properly registered client/secret (via sasjs auth).

The sasjs auth login command authenticates against a SAS Viya target using a regular SAS username and password - no registered OAuth client/secret is required. It uses the password grant against the built-in, secret-less sas.cli public client (the same client used by the official SAS Viya CLI), and the resulting token carries full user impersonation.

sasjs auth login -t myviyatarget

Additional arguments may include:

  • --target (alias -t) - the target environment to authenticate against.
  • --insecure (alias -i) - bypass TLS certificate validation, for Viya servers with self-signed certificates (mirrors the --insecure flag on sasjs add cred). For a permanent fix, prefer the httpsAgentOptions configuration described in TLS Config.

You will be prompted for your username and password (the password input is masked). The password is never stored - it is exchanged directly for an ACCESS_TOKEN / REFRESH_TOKEN pair, which is verified (against /identities/users/@currentUser) and then persisted exactly as with the regular sasjs auth flow (.env.[target name] for local targets, ~/.sasjsrc for global targets).

All authenticated commands (sasjs run, sasjs deploy, sasjs job execute, sasjs flow, sasjs fs, sasjs request, sasjs context, sasjs folder, sasjs test) then work exactly as before - no client/secret is ever needed.

Example:

sasjs auth login -t viya
# Username: viyademo01
# Password: ********
# Logged in as viyademo01 (Viya Demo User)

sasjs run myprogram.sas -t viya

docs.title: Token expiry and refresh
docs.text:
The CLI automatically refreshes the access token using the stored refresh token (via the sas.cli client) whenever it is close to expiry - this works with or without a registered client/secret. If the refresh token itself expires (or is rejected by the server), simply run sasjs auth login -t <target> again.

Note

Some estates issue short-lived access tokens for the sas.cli client (e.g. 1 hour instead of the usual 12), which means a silent refresh happens on most invocations. This is normal and harmless. Note also that Viya refresh tokens are single-use and rotate on every refresh - the CLI persists the rotated pair automatically after every refresh, including refreshes that happen inside long-running job executions.

docs.title: Requirements and limitations
docs.text:
• The password grant must be enabled for the sas.cli client (the default on Viya 3.5+ and Viya 4).
  • The account must be a local or LDAP account - sasjs auth login cannot work on SSO/SAML/MFA-only estates.
  • If the estate has self-signed certificates, use the --insecure flag or configure httpsAgentOptions as described in TLS Config below.
  • On a cold Viya estate, the first compute session creation can take several minutes (pod spin-up) - the first sasjs run may appear to hang. Subsequent runs are fast.
  • If sasjs run fails with a 403 when creating a compute session, your account may not be authorised for the configured compute context - try setting contextName: "SAS Studio compute context" on the target.

docs.title: SAS 9 Authentication
docs.text:
SAS 9 authentication requires a username and password. We strongly recommend the use of SAS encoded passwords (method=sas003 and above), however - to enable this you will first need to make a server side change (to the AllowEncodedPassword property) as follows:

  1. Log on to SAS® Management Console.
  2. Select Application Management.
  3. Navigate to Configuration Manager ► Stored Process Web App
  4. Select Properties ► Advanced (tab).
  5. Click the Add button and define a new property:
    • Property Name: AllowEncodedPassword
    • Property Value: true
  6. Click OK
  7. Restart the Mid Tier Web Server

If the password you provide is not sas-encoded, the command will still work, however you will get health warnings in the log.

docs.title: SASjs Runner
docs.text:
SAS 9 operations require the use of a "runner" for executing the SAS code generated by the CLI. For security, this runner is always stored in your home directory in metadata.

To deploy the runner:

/* import the macros */
filename mc url "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sasjs/core/main/all.sas";
%inc mc;
/* create the runner */
filename ft15f001 temp;
parmcards4;
%macro sasjs_runner();
%if %symexist(_webin_fileref) %then %do;
%inc &_webin_fileref;
%end;
%mend sasjs_runner;
%sasjs_runner()
;;;;
%mm_createwebservice(
  path=/User Folders/&sysuserid/My Folder/sasjs,
  name=runner
)

docs.title: SASJS Server Authentication
docs.text: Authentication on SASjs Server is only necessary in server mode (there is no authentication in desktop mode). The default clientID is clientID1.

docs.title: TLS Config
docs.text:
If the server certificates are set up correctly (full chain) then no additional config is required. However, sometimes when there are self-signed certificates, the following error may occur:

unable to verify the first certificate

It means that the webserver you are connecting to is misconfigured (certificate chain is incomplete) and did not include the intermediate certificate.

To resolve, you may step through the following. Replace "4gl.viyacloud.sas.com" with your own SAS server URL.

# 1. grap the logcertfile
openssl s_client -connect 4gl.viyacloud.sas.com:443 -servername 4gl.viyacloud.sas.com | tee logcertfile
# 2. obtain the issuer URI
openssl x509 -in logcertfile -noout -text | grep -i "issuer"
# 3. Fetch CRT from URI above
# for this case, using "http://cacerts.digicert.com/DigiCertTLSRSASHA2562020CA1-1.crt"
curl --output intermediate.crt http://cacerts.digicert.com/DigiCertTLSRSASHA2562020CA1-1.crt
# 4. extract intermediate.pem from the CRT file
openssl x509 -inform DER -in intermediate.crt -out intermediate.pem -text

If you don't have a well-formed URI in step 3 above, you might try step 4 directly on the CRT if you are able to find it. One option is to look in the browser (click the padlock) or check the filesystem - here is a possible location on a Viya platform: /opt/sas/viya/config/etc/SASSecurityCertificateFramework/tls/certs.

Further information on this topic is available in this StackOverflow thread: https://stackoverflow.com/a/60020493

Once you have the PEM file it can be added to the httpsAgentOptions configuration as follows:

For testing, if you are running internally and you trust the target server, you may consider the following property in your sasjs/sasjsconfig.json file to temporarily ignore the certificate errors. However, this is not a recommended approach.

      "httpsAgentOptions": {
        "allowInsecureRequests": true
      }

docs.title: sasjs build
docs.text:
For ease of project deployment, sasjs build brings all the compiled Jobs / Services / Tests together into a single file. Actually, 3 files, as follows:

  • sasjsbuild/target.json - used to deploy using the APIs in Viya or SASjs Server
  • sasjsbuild/target.json.zip - used for faster uploads of large payloads in SASjs Server
  • sasjsbuild/target.sas - used to create the project in SAS 9 or Viya (when no access token is available)

The filename corresponds to the target name unless buildOutputFileName is specified.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
sasjs build [options]

sasjs build takes one option:

Option Alias Description --target -t The target whose configuration drives the build. Defaults to the defaultTarget in sasjsconfig.json.

Examples:

sasjs build -t myTarget

# the same, using the alias
sasjs b -t myTarget

Nothing else is passed on the commandline: the artefact name, the folders and any streamed web content all come from the target's configuration - see sasjsconfig. To run the compile step and the build step together, use sasjs cb; to add the deployment, sasjs cbd.

If a jobs or services folder does not exist in the temporary sasjsbuild folder, then the sasjs compile step is also executed. The alias to run both compile and build steps is sasjs cb.

The benefit of having a seperate command to prepare the build artefacts (rather than bundling it into sasjs compile) is that you can then modify the compiled outputs to ensure you have the build you want - for example, removing tests for a production deploy. If you don't need such changes, then you can just run sasjs cb as a shortcut for both sasjs compile and sasjs build.

docs.title: Target.JSON Build Artefact
docs.text: The JSON file is used by the sasjs deploy command for the SASVIYA serverType to create all the necessary folders, jobs, services & tests (and streamed web apps) in the target appLoc.

docs.title: Target.json.ZIP Build Artefact
docs.text: This is simply a zipped version of the target.json file, and is used when uploading apps or deploying projects to SASjs Server.

docs.title: Target.SAS Build Artefact
docs.text: The generated SAS program can be executed directly in SAS 9 or SAS Viya to create all the jobs/services/tests programmatically. This is especially useful for Viya developers who are unable to obtain a client / secret. For SAS 9 it is the primary deployment method.

docs.title: SAS 9 Build Script
docs.text: The SAS 9 Build Program can be executed in EG or SAS Studio, and also automatically as part of sasjs deploy when deployServicePack is true. You just need to have a runner in your metadata home directory, and to provide credentials using sasjs auth.

docs.title: Viya Build Script
docs.text: The .sas file can be executed in SASStudioV without modification as proc http will use the oauth_bearer=sas_services option to authenticate to the APIs. This is the way to deploy SASjs projects when you do not have a CLIENT or SECRET.

docs.title: Running Viya Build Script in Non-Viya-Enabled SAS sessions
docs.text:
If for some reason you need to run the Viya build script in a non SPRE / Viya-enabled session (eg in SAS 9 or SASjs Server) you will need to prepare the access token - see guidance here: https://cli.sasjs.io/faq/#viya-token-macros

Put this access token in a macro variable called ACCESS_TOKEN and it will be used by proc http in the core macros by reference to the access_token_var= keyword parameter of each viya macro (the ones that start with mv*).

Warning

Saving security tokens in project repositories, especially if they are committed to source control, is a security risk - as anyone with access can use them to make modifications on the Viya platform. If you are running Viya code in non Viya-enabled SAS environments using the ACCESS_TOKEN approach described above, be sure to use a secure mechanism such as %inc from a secure directory, or another approved mechanism for securing these kinds of variables. Avoid writing Access Tokens to log files.

docs.title: Browser build (streamConfig.mockWeb)
docs.text:
Setting mockWeb to true makes sasjs build produce a second artefact: a self-contained static site whose backend runs in the browser. The same services run, the same webout and header contract applies, and there is no server, no SAS and no network in the path. It exists so an app whose services are JavaScript can be hosted on any static host - a demo, a review environment, a shared link - and still behave like a deployed SASjs app.

"streamConfig": {
  "webSourcePath": "../client/dist",
  "mockWeb": true,
  "mockWebFolder": "sasjsbuild/mock"
}

mockWeb is independent of streamWeb: the same target still deploys for real, so one config serves both the browser build and a normal sasjs deploy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• the target's services must be JavaScript - typically the mocks project pattern, where sas/mocks/sasjs/services holds .js programs. A target that compiles .sas cannot be built for the browser, and the build says so
  • webSourcePath has to point at the built frontend (dist by default); the site is assembled from that folder
  • the target's appLoc has to match the appLoc the frontend was built with, because the services are resolved from it

docs.title: What the build produces
docs.text: The site is written to mockWebFolder, sasjsbuild/mock by default. It contains the frontend, the compiled JavaScript services, a service worker and the small runtime that executes them. The virtual drive the services see is seeded from the build output - the same files sasjs compile wrote, plus anything syncFolder copied in - so a service reading services/... or a data file finds it without any upload step.

docs.title: How it runs
docs.text: A service worker intercepts the calls the SASjs Adapter makes, invokes the matching JavaScript service, and resolves webout, log and headers back to the app. Requests appear in the browser's network tab as they normally would. Anything the services write to the drive is kept in IndexedDB, so a page refresh does not lose it.

docs.title: Downloads and file responses
docs.text:
A service answers with a file the same way it does on a server: it declares the response in _SASJS_WEBOUT_HEADERS and writes the body where the wrapper points it. The generated wrapper already declares fs, so a service uses it rather than requiring it again.

For text - a CSV, a DDL script, a log - assign _webout (or write the string to weboutPath):

fs.writeFileSync(
  _SASJS_WEBOUT_HEADERS,
  'Content-type: text/csv\nContent-Disposition: attachment;filename="users.csv"'
)
_webout = 'id,name\n1,Ann\n'

For bytes - a zip, an xlsx, an image - write them to weboutPath as a Buffer or a Uint8Array:

fs.writeFileSync(
  _SASJS_WEBOUT_HEADERS,
  'Content-type: application/zip\nContent-Disposition: attachment;filename="pack.zip"'
)
fs.writeFileSync(weboutPath, Buffer.from(zipBytes))

Buffer.from() takes bytes, an array of numbers, or a base64 string with 'base64' as the second argument, so a library that produces base64 needs no extra step. This is the browser counterpart of %mp_streamfile - the same two writes - and the browser offers the response under the name in Content-Disposition.

Only Content-type and Content-Disposition are applied; any other header is ignored, because a static host has no cache to control and no cookies to set. A request made with _debug returns the text frame instead, since its body is the webout wrapped in the log.

Some things to keep in mind:

  • the drive holds text, so a file a service writes as bytes is stored as base64 and reads back as bytes - it is a demo drive, not a filesystem for large binaries
  • with no Content-type declared, a byte body is served as application/octet-stream
  • a filename outside ASCII belongs in RFC 6266 form - Content-Disposition: attachment;filename*=UTF-8''r%C3%A9sum%C3%A9.csv. Raw non-ASCII bytes in a header are not portable: the browser's own download honours the bytes it is given, and the same header sent by a SASjs Server arrives with node's latin1 encoding, so the two only agree on the ASCII form

docs.title: Serving it
docs.text:
Serve the folder over http or https. A service worker needs a secure context, which means localhost and https both work but file:// does not:

cd sasjsbuild/mock
python3 -m http.server 8099

Deploy it like any static site - it is just files. The runtime files under host/ are referenced with a ?v=<hash> query that changes with their contents, so a redeploy replaces them for returning visitors too; upload index.html and sw.js together with everything else, since those two carry the reference.

docs.title: Shipping the site with data
docs.text:
Out of the box the drive a visitor gets holds the services and whatever else lives in the build folder - enough to run, but empty of the data those services would have produced. A snapshot changes that: if mock-snapshot.json sits in the build folder, the build copies it to host/vfs-snapshot.json and the runtime prefers it over the plain seed, so every visitor starts from the captured state instead of an empty drive.

To capture one, open the site, use the app until the drive is in the state you want, and run this in the browser console:

await window.SASjsMock.download()

That saves mock-snapshot.json to your downloads. Put it beside the compiled output - sasjsbuild/mock-snapshot.json for the default build folder - and build again. The build reports it in host/mock-config.json as "snapshot": true.

{
  "appLoc": "/Public/app/dc",
  "snapshot": true,
  "driveEntries": 97,
  "jsPrograms": 43
}

Three things worth knowing:

  • the snapshot is a plain JSON map of drive path to file contents, and a real app's drive runs to megabytes, so treat it as a build input you generate rather than something to keep in git
  • state stays tied to where it was captured. A licence issued for one origin does not decrypt on another, so capture the snapshot on the domain you deploy to - if an app asks to be licensed or configured after deployment while it worked locally, this is the usual reason
  • to start over, window.SASjsMock.reset() clears the persisted drive and reseeds from the shipped files; to ship the plain seed instead, remove mock-snapshot.json from the build folder and build again

Warning

This is a single-user, no-authentication build. Services that read SAS tables, run macros or depend on SAS libraries cannot work in it, because there is no SAS engine in the browser. Treat it as a demo and review artefact, not as a replacement for a real deployment.

docs.title: sasjs cb
docs.text: sasjs cb runs sasjs compile, and then sasjs build. It is the shortcut for the two steps that produce a deployable artefact, without the deployment that sasjs cbd adds.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
sasjs cb [options]

sasjs compilebuild is the long form of the same command.

Option Alias Description --target -t The target whose configuration drives the compile and the build. Defaults to the defaultTarget in sasjsconfig.json.

Examples:

sasjs cb -t myTarget
sasjs compilebuild -t myTarget

docs.title: What it runs
docs.text:
Step Command Output 1 sasjs compile sasjsbuild/jobs, sasjsbuild/services, sasjsbuild/tests 2 sasjs build sasjsbuild/<target>.json, .json.zip and .sas

A compile that fails stops the run - the build is not attempted, and the command exits with an error. When both succeed, the compile and build output is in the sasjsbuild folder, ready for sasjs deploy.

docs.title: When to use the two commands separately
docs.text:
sasjs cb leaves no opportunity to change the compiled output between the two steps. If you want to adjust what gets built - removing tests for a production deploy, for instance - run the commands yourself:

sasjs compile -t myTarget
rm -rf sasjsbuild/tests
sasjs build -t myTarget

docs.title: sasjs cbd
docs.text:
The sasjs cbd command is actually an alias for three commands, namely:

  1. sasjs compile
  2. sasjs build
  3. sasjs deploy

If you are changing a source file, then it is typically necessary to run all three commands in order to get your project deployed, so sasjs cbd is a handy shortcut.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
sasjs cbd [options]

sasjs compilebuilddeploy is the long form of the same command.

Option Alias Description --target -t The target whose configuration drives all three steps. Defaults to the defaultTarget in sasjsconfig.json.

Examples:

sasjs cbd -t myTarget
sasjs compilebuilddeploy -t myTarget

If you only want the artefact - not the deployment - use sasjs cb, which runs sasjs compile and sasjs build and stops there.

Sometimes though you need to run separately - for example, say you would like to deploy to a production but without the tests.

You could run sasjs compile first (which includes the tests), then rm -rf sasjsbuild/tests, then sasjs build (without tests) and finally sasjs deploy.

Or perhaps you have run sasjs cbd but the process failed during deployment due to an authorisation issue. You can simply run sasjs auth (to re-authorise) and then sasjs deploy (to avoid the recompilation and rebuild).

The following diagram illustrates the end to end sasjs cbd process.

Notes:

  • Source code is organised however you like within the GIT repository
  • sasjs compile pulls all the dependencies to create self-contained jobs, services & tests
  • These live within a .gitignore'd folder called sasjsbuild in the project repo
  • sasjs build takes all the compiled artefacts to create a "build pack" (in .sas and .json formats)
  • This build pack can now be used to easily deploy the project to the target SAS environment.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Compilation in SASjs is driven from the sasjs/sasjsconfig.json file, and results in the creation of a single self-contained SAS program per JOB / SERVICE / TEST.

The benefits of working with compiled files are severalfold:

  • Build on ONE platform, deploy to THREE (Viya, EBI, Base)
  • Elimination of SAS Catalogs for macros / programs
  • Elimination of filesystem dependency for code
  • Resilient and Highly Portable Applications
  • Consistent Performance
  • Easy to debug & test

sasjs compile can be applied to a single file, or more commonly, to all the files in a project.

Content is added to each compiled Job/Service/Test in the following order:

  1. MacroVars
  2. Binary Files
  3. Macros
  4. Programs
  5. initProgram
  6. Job/Service/Test
  7. termProgram

The following diagram illustrates the compilation of a Service (service_xyz.sas) that includes some macro variables, as well as common macro dependencies across the initProgram and termProgram:

Notice that only one copy of the macro is inserted, even though it is defined in multiple artefacts.

The following diagram illustrates the logic flow when compiling a Primary Artefact:

docs.title: 1. sasjsbuild Folder
docs.text:
In every SASjs project, content is split according to whether the file type is Job, Service or Test. For a project that has all three, and has tests covering SAS Macros / Jobs / Tests, the sasjsbuild folder (and ultimately, the remote SAS folder) will contain the following tree:

  • jobs/
  • services/
  • tests/jobs/
  • tests/macros/
  • tests/services/

Below the above, the immediate child will be the last child of the xxxFolder - eg for a serviceConfig as follows:

{
  "serviceConfig":{
    "serviceFolders":[
      "/some/project/location"
    ]
  }
}

A filepath of /some/project/location/myservice.sas will thus be compiled inside: services/location/myservice.sas.

Nested directories are supported. For a filepath of /some/project/location/subfolder/subsubfolder/here.sas the compile location would be: services/location/subfolder/subsubfolder/here.sas.

docs.title: 2. Macro Variables
docs.text:
Macro variables are inserted according to the type of the compiled file, ie from one of the following objects:

  • jobConfig
  • serviceConfig
  • testConfig

docs.title: 3. Binary Files
docs.text: Binary Files are converted to a base64 string and wrapped in put statements with a user provided fileref as described here

docs.title: 4. SAS Macros
docs.text:
SAS Macros are recursively compiled to ensure there is only one copy of each macro across the initProgram, termProgram, the primary artefact itself, and the webout() macros (if a Service or Test).

More info here.

docs.title: 5. SAS Includes
docs.text:
SAS Includes are wrapped in put statements and a filename statement is generated with a user provided fileref.

More info here.

docs.title: 6. initProgram
docs.text:
The initProgram executes right before the main Job / Service / Test.

More info here.

docs.title: 7. Source Code
docs.text:
This section contains the actual code inside the Job / Service / Test.

More info here.

docs.title: Compile Single File
docs.text: A single file can be compiled without compiling the rest of the project. The file type decides the pre-code that wraps it, so either name the type - job, service or test - or pass identify and let the file decide: a *.test.sas name means a test, a path inside a serviceConfig.serviceFolders folder means a service, and a path inside a jobConfig.jobFolders folder means a job. identify needs those folders to be configured - service and job folders are read from the serviceConfig and jobConfig objects, not from top level keys.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
sasjs compile <action> --source <file> [additional arguments]

action can be job, service, test or identify

Additional arguments include:

  • --source (alias -s) - the path of the individual .sas file to compile. MANDATORY
  • --target (alias -t) - The target to use for obtaining the source folders of programs and macros. If it is not specified, the default target will be used, mentioned in sasjsconfig.json. The target can exist either in the local project configuration or in the global .sasjsrc file. OPTIONAL
  • --output (alias -o) - a folder to write the compiled file below instead of sasjsbuild. The structure described under Destination is kept, so the file lands at <output>/jobs/..., <output>/services/... or <output>/tests/.... OPTIONAL.

docs.title: Destination
docs.text:
The compiled file is written where a project compile would put the same file, so the two commands agree:

  • a job goes to sasjsbuild/jobs/<folder name>/<path below that folder>/
  • a service goes to sasjsbuild/services/<folder name>/<path below that folder>/
  • a test goes to sasjsbuild/tests/services|jobs|macros/<folder name>/<path below that folder>/, the sub folder following where the test lives

The <folder name> is the last segment of the serviceConfig.serviceFolders or jobConfig.jobFolders entry that contains the file, and <path below that folder> is the file's own path under it. A file that sits outside every configured folder has no folder name to use and is written straight into the type folder.

Nothing is deleted: the compiled file replaces its own previous copy, so other compiled artefacts in sasjsbuild stay where they are.

sasjs compile job --source sasjs/jobs/admin/somejob.sas
sasjs compile identify --source sasjs/services/common/appinit.sas -t myTarget
sasjs c service --source sasjs/services/common/appinit.sas -o compiledjobs/folder

The output is a full compile of that one file - the same macro variables, inlined dependencies and init / term programs a project compile would give it.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
sasjs compile [additional arguments]

Additional arguments include:

  • --target (alias -t) - The target to use for obtaining the source folders of programs and macros. If it is not specified, default target will be used, mentioned in sasjsconfig.json. The target can exist either in the local project configuration or in the global .sasjsrc file. OPTIONAL

Examples:

sasjs compile
sasjs c
sasjs c -t someTarget

docs.title: Artefact Compilation
docs.text:
From the root of the project, run: sasjs compile. This will cycle through all the Jobs / Services / Tests in the jobFolders / serviceFolders / testFolders arrays in the sasjsconfig.json file, extract all of the dependent Binary Files, SAS Macros, SAS Includes, and create one self-contained file per Job (or Service, or Test) inside the sasjsbuild folder. The self-contained file will also include any initProgram, termProgram and macroVars defined in the relevant config objects.

The binaryFolders, macroFolders and programFolders arrays are searched for Binary Files, SAS Macros and SAS Includes (first in the target config, then in the root).

The serviceConfig, jobConfig and testConfig objects may have attributes split at either or both target and root level in the sasjsconfig.json file.

docs.title: Tests compilation
docs.text:
As part of compilation process test files will be compiled as well. Test configuration should be provided in sasjs/sasjsconfig.json. Test files should be placed in the same folders with services, jobs and macros. Compiled test files will result in sasjsbuild/tests folder under services,jobs or macros subfolder respectively. Tests execution flow will be described in sasjsbuild/testFlow.json file.

Test coverage is written to sasjsbuild/coverage.json alongside testFlow.json. The file carries the totals the console prints under summary, and a files map keyed by project-relative path (macros/myMacro.sas, services/common/myService.sas) in which every compiled service, job and macro is marked covered or not covered, plus any standalone tests. A pipeline can therefore publish the figures or fail a build on a threshold without scraping the log. A project with no compiled tests writes no coverage file.

The testConfig object allows two additional programs to be compiled (as tests):

  • testSetUp - executed once at the beginning of the test run
  • testTearDown - executed once, at the end of the test run

docs.title: SyncFolder Compilation
docs.text: If the syncFolder attribute is set, then the contents of that folder will be simply copied into the sasjsbuild folder. This is useful for providing mocked services (eg in sasjs/server) or to add arbitrary content to the SAS logical folder tree.

docs.title: Streaming Apps
docs.text: If streamWeb is true, then the index.html file in your webSourcePath is also scanned and any linked JS / CSS files are also compiled into the streamWebFolder folder. The index.html becomes a clickme service in your appLoc SAS folder root.

docs.title: Base64 encoding
docs.text: If you don't have an index.html and you just want to compile arbitrary binary content (such as images, mp3, excel files etc) as base64 services, set the location of the content in assetPaths. All files in the specified folder(s) will be turned into web services.

docs.title: sasjs context
docs.text:
The sasjs context command allows users to list all and export individual Compute Contexts. Administrators may also create, edit and delete contexts.

A compute context is used when firing up a new SAS session (it itself inherits from a Launcher Context). Example use cases for this tool:

  • Creating a new compute context as part of a CI/CD deploy
  • Deleting a compute context as part of a tidy up
  • Discovering which compute contexts can actually be used
  • Modifying a compute context, eg to update the autoexec or system account used

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Before using this command, you will need to install the SASJS CLI and add a deployment target.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
sasjs context <action> [additional arguments]

Additional arguments include:

Option Alias Sub commands Description --source -s create, edit The JSON file holding the context definition. Required for both. --target -t all The target whose server holds the contexts. SAS Viya only. Defaults to defaultTarget in sasjsconfig.json, then the global .sasjsrc.

docs.title: Compute Context Structure
docs.text:
The create and edit actions use the same JSON structure for adding / modifying contexts. This also matches the context made by the export action, which can be used to provide a template for adding / modifying new contexts. The JSON is defined as follows:

{
  "name": "myNewComputeContext",
  "attributes": {
    "reuseServerProcesses": true,
    "runServerAs": "mycasaccount"
  },
  "environment": {
    "autoExecLines": [
      "%put autoexec line 1;",
      "%put autoexect line 2;"
    ],
    "options": [
     "-BUFNO 10",
     "-MEMSIZE 4G"
    ]
  },
  "launchContext": {
    "contextName": "SAS Job Execution launcher context"
  },
  "launchType": "service",
}

To explain the sections:

  • name - name of the compute context you will create
  • reuseServerProcesses - since Viya 3.5 you can re-use sessions, this improves performance significantly but requires the sessions to run under a system account (defined below)
  • runServerAs - the system account to use when re-using server processes
  • autoExecLines - an array of SAS program lines. These will execute ONCE when the server process is started, so expensive libname assignments could be placed here, speeding up web service response times.
  • options - an array of SAS option settings
  • contextName - the name of the launcher context used to spawn the compute context
  • launchtype - a mandatory parameter, more details here

docs.title: sasjs context create
docs.text: Used to create a new compute context.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: sasjs context create -s source.json -t target

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# create minimal context config
cat > ./myContext.json <<'EOL'
{
  "name": "myNewComputeContext",
  "launchContext": {
    "contextName": "SAS Job Execution launcher context"
  },
  "launchType": "service"
}
EOL

# create the context using the target defined in sasjs add
sasjs context create -s ./myContext.json -t myTarget

docs.title: sasjs context delete
docs.text: Used to delete an existing context. No source JSON needed, contextName is used instead.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: sasjs context delete <contextName> -t target

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: sasjs context delete myUndesirableComputeContext -t myTarget

docs.title: sasjs context edit
docs.text: Used to edit an existing context

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: sasjs context edit <contextName> -s source.json -t target

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# create JSON file with the changes to apply
cat > ./myContext.json <<'EOL'
{
  "name": "myRenamedComputeContext",
  "launchContext": {
    "contextName": "Some Other launcher context"
  },
  "launchType": "service"
}
EOL

# update the context named myComputeContext
sasjs context edit myComputeContext -s ./myContext.json -t myTarget

docs.title: sasjs context export
docs.text: Exports specified compute context to contextName.json in the current folder. No source JSON is needed, just provide the contextName.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: sasjs context export <contextName> -t target

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: sasjs context export someContext -t myTarget

docs.title: sasjs context list
docs.text: Outputs a list of all accessible and inaccessible contexts. Accessible contexts are discovered by attempting to run %put &=sysuserid; on each context.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: sasjs context list -t target

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: sasjs context list -t myTarget

docs.title: sasjs create
docs.text: sasjs create scaffolds a SASjs project: the folder structure, a sasjs/sasjsconfig.json to go with it, the doxygen templates, the lint config, a README and a .gitignore.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
sasjs create [folder-name] [options]
Option Alias Description --template -t The template to scaffold from. One of react, angular, minimal, sasonly or jobs. Omitted, the command writes the plain folder structure instead.

Warning

-t is the template here, not the target used by most other commands. There is no target option on sasjs create - a new project needs no connection to a SAS server.

Examples:

# a plain SASjs project
sasjs create my-sas-project

# a React app, with the SASjs backend and the adapter wired up
sasjs create my-web-app --template react
sasjs create my-web-app -t react

docs.title: The plain project
docs.text:
With no --template, sasjs create writes the structure below, and then runs npm init and adds @sasjs/core as a dependency.

my-sas-project/
└── sasjs/
    ├── sasjsconfig.json     <- three targets: viya, sas9 and sasjs
    ├── build/               <- init/term programs, and the deploy scripts
    ├── db/                  <- one folder per database, with example DDL and load programs
    ├── macros/              <- your SAS macros
    ├── programs/            <- SAS programs included by services
    ├── services/            <- SASjs web services (common/ and admin/)
    └── targets/             <- per-target macros, services and programs
        ├── sas9/
        └── viya/

The generated sasjsconfig.json configures serviceFolders, macroFolders and buildConfig against those folders, and carries the three placeholder targets, so the project can be compiled and built without editing anything. Put the real server details into a target with sasjs add before you deploy.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text: Template Source What you get react sasjs/react-seed-app A React app, with the SASjs Adapter configured and a SASjs backend angular sasjs/angular-seed-app The same, in Angular minimal sasjs/minimal-seed-app A small app in plain JavaScript jobs sasjs/template_jobs Backend only: SAS jobs, with a flow example sasonly sasjs/template_sasonly Backend only: SAS web services, no frontend

docs.title: Running it in an existing folder
docs.text:
Run sasjs create with no folder name and the project is written into the current directory - the folder structure is created there, and package.json gains the @sasjs/core dependency if the folder already holds one.

If the folder already contains SAS code that you want to keep, use sasjs init instead: it adds the SASjs tooling without writing a folder structure over what is there.

docs.title: sasjs db
docs.text:
sasjs db gathers the database scripts of a project into one program per database. Each sub folder of sasjs/db is treated as a database, and its files are concatenated into sasjsbuild/db/<database>.<extension>.

The command exists so that a database build can be run as a single SAS program - the same shape as the compiled jobs and services - rather than as a folder of loose scripts.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
sasjs db

sasjs build-DB and sasjs build-db are accepted as alternative names for the same command.

The command takes no options. It works on the project it is run in, reading sasjs/db and writing below the project's build folder.

Warning

In CLI 6.4.7 and earlier the command fails before writing anything, with Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'buildSourceDbFolder') - it never resolves the target, so the build folders are unset. Fix in sasjs/cli#1525 (reported as sasjs/cli#1524). That release also adds --target (-t), which picks the target whose sasjsBuildFolder the output goes into; this page gains the option when the release is out.

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
Every immediate sub folder of sasjs/db is a database. Only two file extensions are read: .ddl and .sas. Other files in the folder are ignored.

sasjs/db/
├── sales.ini          <- optional, prefixed to the sales DDL
├── sales/
│   ├── 01-tables.ddl
│   ├── 02-views.ddl
│   └── 03-load.sas
└── warehouse/
    └── 01-tables.ddl

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Path Contains sasjsbuild/db/sales.ddl The contents of sales.ini (when present), then every .ddl file of sales/, in folder order sasjsbuild/db/sales.sas Every .sas file of sales/ sasjsbuild/db/warehouse.ddl Every .ddl file of warehouse/

Notes:

  • the .ini file is placed beside the database folder and shares its name - sasjs/db/<database>.ini - and is prepended to the .ddl output only
  • the db folder in the build destination is recreated on every run, so a deleted source file does not linger in an old build
  • the extension is the last segment of the file name, so 01-tables.ddl counts as .ddl

The result is plain SAS code, so it can be executed like any other program - %include it from a deployment script, or run it with sasjs run.

docs.title: sasjs deploy
docs.text:
Deploy to multiple servers, server types (Viya, EBI, Base), multiple folders (Drive or Metadata) within those folders, and with multiple configurations, each with a simple alias - a target name.

The ability to easily deploy (and subsequently execute) your SAS code enables you to develop locally using established GIT workflows.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before using this command, you will need to install the SASJS CLI and:

  • add a deployment target.
  • compile services.
  • build services.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
The build program generated in the previous step can be deployed in 3 ways:

1 - MANUAL: copy paste the code into Studio or Enterprise Guide and run it

2 - SSH: build a shell script or bat file to load, and execute with a web service

3 - API: use the SAS APIs

2nd and 3rd options can be configured and executed with a single command:

sasjs deploy [options]
Option Alias Description --target -t The target to deploy to. Defaults to defaultTarget in sasjsconfig.json; if there is no project config, the global .sasjsrc is used.

Examples:

sasjs deploy -t myTarget
sasjs d -t myTarget

To compile, build and deploy in one step, use sasjs cbd.

NOTE: By default deploy will overwrite an existing deploy (force deploy).

docs.title: Copy/Paste approach
docs.text:
The build script (named as per buildOutputFileName) can be copy pasted into SAS Studio and executed to create the backend services. Please note:

  • You will be running under your own identity. If you need files created under the Web Server identity, deploy your build script using a web service.
  • For Viya, you must use SASStudioV (or ensure the client/secret/access_token are provided)

docs.title: SSH approach
docs.text:
You can SSH (rsync or scp) your build script onto the SAS Server then %inc it from a web service - the web service could be created using the code below:

filename mc url "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sasjs/core/main/all.sas";
%inc mc;
